name: Robinhood
tagline: Commission-free brokerage app for stocks, options, and crypto, with a paid Gold tier.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: You cannot build a broker-dealer in an afternoon, and you should not want to. The product is a regulated entity that holds your money, routes orders to market makers, clears and settles trades, files with FINRA and the SEC, and carries SIPC coverage. The app itself is a thin, pretty client on top of all that, and yes, the client is copyable. What you can actually one-shot is the part you care about between trades: a local portfolio tracker that pulls quotes, computes cost basis and unrealized gains, and shows you the number without a confetti animation. Executing the trade still happens at a licensed broker, whether that is Robinhood or someone else.
coreLoopDIY: A local dashboard where you enter your holdings and transactions, pull daily quotes from a market data API, and see positions, cost basis, allocation, and gain/loss over time.
requirements: A market data API key, free tiers exist and are rate limited
Manual entry or CSV import of your own transaction history
An actual licensed brokerage account to place the trades
whatYouLose: Order execution, clearing, settlement, and custody of your assets
SIPC coverage and the regulatory apparatus behind it
Real-time streaming quotes, options chains, and margin
Tax documents: 1099-B, cost basis reporting, wash sale handling
Mobile app, instant deposits, fractional shares, retirement account matching
moatNotes: The confetti was never the product. Being allowed to hold other people's money is.
whyPeopleStillPay: Almost nobody pays Robinhood for the interface. They pay Gold for margin rates, a higher cash yield, research access, and an IRA match, and they use the free tier because it is a legally licensed place to buy a share of stock in three taps. Order routing revenue and net interest income fund the rest. Replacing the app is a UI exercise; replacing the broker means capital requirements, audits, and a compliance department.
notes: The dashboard is a one-sitting build; the license to hold your cash is not. The moat is being a registered broker-dealer with clearing, custody, and SIPC coverage attached.
prompt:
Build a local-only personal portfolio tracker. This is a read-only tracker, NOT a trading app: no order placement, no broker connection, no custody of funds.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Next.js with the App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, single file at ./data/portfolio.db
- Recharts for charts
- Runs with `npm run dev` on localhost, no auth, no accounts, no telemetry

Data model:
- accounts: id, name, type (taxable, ira, crypto)
- transactions: id, accountId, symbol, type (buy, sell, dividend, split, deposit, withdrawal), quantity, pricePerUnit, fees, tradedAt, notes
- quotes: symbol, date, close (cached daily closes)

Features in scope:
- Manual transaction entry form plus a CSV importer with a column mapping step
- Derive current positions from the transaction ledger, do not store positions directly
- Cost basis with a switchable method: FIFO or average cost. Show realized and unrealized gain/loss per position and in total
- Fetch daily closes from a market data provider using MARKET_DATA_API_KEY from .env, cache them in the quotes table, never refetch a date already stored, and degrade gracefully to the last cached close when the API fails or rate limits
- Dashboard: total value, total cost, unrealized gain/loss, allocation pie by symbol and by account, and a portfolio value line chart built by replaying the ledger against cached closes
- Dividend income view grouped by year
- Export everything back out to CSV

Explicitly out of scope: real-time or streaming quotes, options, margin, tax form generation, wash sale rules, multi-user support, mobile apps, push notifications.

Write a README that names the market data provider, explains the .env variable, states the cost basis method limitations in plain language, and says clearly that this file is not tax advice and not a brokerage.
